title: Bài sưu tầm 101 - Passage 1: The Antikythera Mechanism: The World's First Computer
passageHtml:
READING PASSAGE 1 — TEST 101

The Antikythera Mechanism: The World's First Computer

Paragraph 1. In the spring of 1900, a crew of Greek sponge divers returning from North Africa was forced off course by an intense gale. Seeking shelter, they dropped anchor near the tiny, barren island of Antikythera, situated between Crete and the Greek mainland. When the storm subsided, diver Elias Stadiatis donned a bronze diving helmet and descended to a depth of 45 metres to search for sponges. Instead of marine life, Stadiatis surfaced trembling, babbling about a seabed covered with rotting corpses and bronze horses. He had stumbled upon an ancient Roman shipwreck dating to the first century BCE, laden with marble statues, pottery, and exquisite bronze sculptures.

Paragraph 2. Over the following nine months, Greek authorities carried out a salvage operation in hazardous deep waters. Among the rescued treasures brought to the National Archaeological Museum in Athens was an unassuming, calcified lump of corroded bronze encrusted with marine sediment. For almost two years, this ugly relic sat unnoticed in an outdoor courtyard. In May 1902, archaeologist Valerios Stais was examining the collection when he noticed that the decaying mass had cracked open, exposing a remarkably intricate gear with triangular teeth embedded inside. Initial academic consensus dismissed the object as an anachronism; classicists insisted that such advanced mechanical design could not have existed in antiquity and speculated that it was an astrolabe or navigation clock dropped by a passing medieval ship.

Paragraph 3. Decades of subsequent multidisciplinary research disproved this skepticism. British physicist Derek de Solla Price began analysing the relic in the 1950s using X-ray photography. His work revealed that the fragments belonged to a single portable device originally enclosed in a protective wooden frame roughly the size of a mantelpiece clock. Inscribed bronze plates had once covered the exterior, acting as an ancient user manual containing operational instructions and calendars. The device, dated to approximately 150–100 BCE, contained at least thirty interlocking bronze gears powered by a hand-turned crank. Turning the crank moved a complex system of differential gears, translating human motion into the calculated movements of celestial bodies.

Paragraph 4. The front dial of the mechanism featured two concentric rings: an inner ring displaying the twelve signs of the zodiac and an outer ring corresponding to the 365 days of the Egyptian solar calendar. Pointers indicated the daily coordinates of the sun and moon, while an ingenious pin-and-slot gear assembly simulated the moon's irregular orbit, precisely matching its fluctuating speed across the night sky. On the reverse side, upper and lower spiral dials tracked the Metonic cycle (a 19-year lunar-solar calendar) and the Saros cycle, a 223-month sequence capable of predicting upcoming eclipses with frightening accuracy, even indicating the hour of the event and the expected colour of the obscured moon.

Paragraph 5. In 2005, the Antikythera Mechanism Research Project applied cutting-edge technology to the heavily fragmented device. Using three-dimensional computed tomography, scientists took high-resolution scans that pierced deep into the corroded bronze cores. This non-destructive technique unveiled thousands of microscopic text characters and faint inscriptions invisible to the naked eye. Crucially, the scans confirmed the presence of gearing designed to track the orbital movements of five known planets—Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn. The Antikythera Mechanism demonstrated that the mechanical sophistication of the Hellenistic world was millennia ahead of what modern historians had ever conceived.

Đoạn 5: "...gearing designed to track the orbital movements of five known planets..."

q8.text: The sponge divers arrived at Antikythera intentionally looking for ancient artifacts.

steps: Đoạn 1: Thợ lặn bị bão dạt vào bờ khi đang đánh bắt hải sản trở về (forced off course by an intense gale), mục đích không phải tìm cổ vật.

q9.text: Early scholars believed the corroded bronze object was too technologically advanced for ancient Greece.

steps: Đoạn 2: "classicists insisted that such advanced mechanical design could not have existed in antiquity..."

q10.text: Derek de Solla Price was the first researcher to identify the exact individual who built the device.

steps: Đoạn 3: Có nhắc đến Price nghiên cứu thiết bị bằng X-ray, nhưng bài đọc hoàn toàn không đề cập việc ông có tìm ra danh tính người chế tạo hay không.

q11.text: The device required continuous water flow to power its internal gear system.

steps: Đoạn 3: "powered by a hand-turned crank" → quay bằng tay quay, mâu thuẫn trực tiếp với chạy bằng sức nước.

q12.text: Microscopic inscriptions inside the mechanism could be seen without using specialized scanning equipment.

steps: Đoạn 5: "...inscriptions invisible to the naked eye" → mắt thường không thể thấy, mâu thuẫn với "without using specialized equipment".

q13.text: The discovery of the mechanism forced historians to revise their opinions on ancient engineering capabilities.

steps: Đoạn 5: "...sophistication of the Hellenistic world was millennia ahead of what modern historians had ever conceived".
